Alejandro Zarzuelo Urdiales   21:31

Hi Woohyuk,

I am helping organize OpenMath at MIT and would love to have your team involved.

Your AI and robotics work at HTPeo made me think this could be an interesting challenge for a small technical team. Would you consider applying those computational skills to mathematical problems for the week?

The goal is to produce a substantial body of useful, formally verified mathematics in one week and explore how far iterative AI research workflows can take us. Open-problem advances and useful new formalizations both have a place.

We are inviting mathematical-AI companies as well as other research teams. Company entries have separate standings, as set out in the handbook. This would be an opportunity to show the mathematical community what your tools can do through public, inspectable results. Accepted contributions will be credited to the teams that produce them.

The kickoff is at MIT CSAIL on Sunday, September 27, 2026, at noon Eastern / 9 a.m. Pacific, with work continuing through Friday, October 2. Teams of up to four can participate entirely online, and opening attendance is not required. Any AI tools, or human-only work, are welcome. Only formally checked and mathematically reviewed results count.

Details, handbook and registration: https://rsihouse.ai/openmath

Please let me know if you have any questions, I would be happy to help.

One week. Open mathematics. Machine-checked results.
rsihouse.ai

Hi! Just following up since we’re now close to the submission deadline and our team wants to make sure we’re working toward the correct acceptance criteria.

Hi Terry,

I am helping organize OpenMath at MIT and wanted to share it with you.

Your AI-inference engineering experience could bring a useful systems perspective to teams running repeated research and checking cycles. Would you be interested in participating personally alongside people focused on the mathematics?

Our ambition is to produce a substantial body of useful, formally verified mathematics in one week, tackling open problems and producing useful new formalizations of known mathematics. We also want to learn which AI research workflows actually help, using the loop of proposing, checking and improving results.

The kickoff is at MIT CSAIL on Sunday, September 27, 2026, at noon Eastern / 9 a.m. Pacific, and the competition runs through Friday, October 2. Participation can be entirely online, individually or in teams of up to four, and attending the opening is not required. Any AI tools, or human-only work, are welcome. Only formally checked and mathematically reviewed results count.

Details, handbook and registration: https://rsihouse.ai/openmath

Please let me know if you have any questions, I would be happy to help.
